subject: Connectivity model recommendation for Silverline Health: peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S (ops tradeoffs)
messages:

Subject: Connectivity options for Silverline private deployment

Hi Lauren,

Thanks again for the walkthrough earlier. We're starting to sketch the network side for the on-prem private deployment and need a short recommendation we can take to NetOps. High level ask: which connectivity model gives us the best mix of operational simplicity, least ongoing maintenance, and acceptable security posture? We're currently evaluating three: VPC peering (where available), AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site VPN.

Attached is a simple network diagram and our initial constraints:
- Multiple on-prem data centers (primary + DR)
- Compliance: SOC2 + HIPAA controls for ePHI
- Expect moderate steady throughput (peak bursts during business hours)
- NetOps wants minimal NAT and no shared CIDR conflicts if possible

Could you and your team outline recommended default, fallback, and what we should ask our network security folks to approve? A short 1-2 pager we can hand off would be ideal.

Appreciate it,
Samir

Attachments: silverline-network-diagram.pdf (diagram, 1 page)

Samir — thanks for the diagram and constraints, useful context. I've looped in Ben (field engineering) and Kim (solutions/netops) to provide a concise recommendation and a short handoff checklist.

High-level summary we're going to send:
- Default (best balance): PrivateLink + minimal S2S for on-prem edge sites where PrivateLink isn't available.
- Low-latency/high-throughput preference: VPC peering where CIDR non-overlap can be guaranteed and both sides run in the same cloud account/region.
- Fallback: IPsec S2S (managed) when peering or PrivateLink aren't feasible (overlapping CIDRs, cross-account limits, or on-prem-only workloads).

We will include: security considerations (TLS + mutual auth, limited egress rules), NAT impacts, operational steps for certificate/key rotation, and runbook items for failover. Expect the memo by EOD tomorrow.

—Lauren

Samir, Sam — quick practical notes from FE ops after reviewing their diagram: 

1) PrivateLink (interface endpoints) — pros/cons- Pros:
  - No CIDR overlap constraints (consumer keeps its CIDR)
  - Strong isolation (only services exposed via ENIs)
  - Works well for regulated traffic because data plane terminates into our VPC (reduces surface area)
- Cons:
  - Operates at service endpoint level — you need to ensure the set of Redwood endpoints covers all necessary APIs/ports
  - Higher per-endpoint ops (ENIs in subnets, limits to manage)
  - Slightly more complex for multi-region or multi-account setups (need interface endpoints per region/account)

2) VPC Peering — pros/cons- Pros:
  - Very low-latency, simple L3 routing across VPCs
  - Minimal extra components — good for high-throughputsteadystate
- Cons:
  - Requires non-overlapping CIDRs (major blocker for many legacy data centers)
  - Not transitive (complicates multi-network topologies)
  - Harder for cross-account unless permissions are well-managed
3) Site-to-site VPN (IPsec) — pros/cons- Pros:
  - Flexible (works with on-prem that can't use cloud-native endpoints)
  - Good fallback option; many customers prefer a managed IPsec appliance
- Cons:
  - Added latency, packetization overhead, and potential throughput cap (unless using higher-end appliances)
  - More operational burdern for key rotation / monitoring
Recommendation (short):
- Recommend starting with PrivateLink for control-plane and sensitive ePHI paths (small number of endpoints).
- Where you need any-to-any L3 connectivity (data replication between on-prem and cloud app subnet), use peering only if CIDRs can be cleaned up; otherwise use S2S for those segments.
- Always provision S2S as a tested fallback.

I'll assemble a one-page matrix with operational steps and HLD notes; including NAT implications (double-NAT risk for peering vs PrivateLink) and a suggested fallback test plan.

—Ben

Adding a short operational checklist for Silverline NetOps to accelerate sign-off: 

Pre-approval items (ask Silverline to confirm):
- Confirm primary CIDR allocations for the on-prem app VLANs (will they overlap with Redwood-managed VPCs?).
- Identify which systems require inbound-initiated connections vs outbound-only API calls (PrivateLink covers outbound/ingress patterns better).
- Provide maintenance windows and DR failover SLA requirements (S2S failover timing matters).

Implementation checklist (Redwood + Silverline):
- PrivateLink plan: select subnets for endpoints (avoid NAT gateway asymmetry), assign security groups that restrict to Silverline ENIs, configure endpoint policies limiting access to required APIs.
- VPC Peering plan: validate route tables, add explicit route entries, and coordinate firewall rules. Execute CIDR conflict resolution if needed (rename/renumber or utilize NAT for problematic ranges).
- S2S plan: define IKEv2 proposals, pre-shared key rotation policy, monitoring (BGP/route health or CloudWatch metrics), and throughput expectations.

Operational notes:
- If Silverline wants a single cohesive approach, PrivateLink for ePHI and S2S for legacy replication is the least operationally expensive to run long term.
- For peering to be viable long-term you must lock down CIDR ownership and commit to preventing overlapping ranges on future projects.

I'll attach the 1-pager in the next mail with diagrams and an explicit runbook (testing steps + rollback).

—Kim

Samir — attaching the final one-pager and the short runbook. TL;DR: go PrivateLink for ePHI APIs + provision an IPsec S2S tunnel between your primary DC and the Redwood VPC as fallback and for any L3 replication traffic. Use VPC peering only if you can guarantee CIDR non-overlap and commit to keeping the peered VPC in the same account/region.

Next steps:
- Silverline: confirm CIDRs and which services need bidirectional L3 vs outbound API-only.
- Redwood: we'll send the PrivateLink endpoint ARNs and a short security policy template you can give NetOps.

Thanks — I'll be on the call Thursday at 11am to walk NetOps through the runbook.

Best,
Lauren
